title: Stain removal: identify, test, treat and record
audience: Trained cleaners who treat stains and spillages on carpets, upholstery and other surfaces in any cleaning-group business, and the supervisors who decide when a stain is referred.
learningOutcomes: Identify the stain and the surface or material before choosing any method.
Remove as much of a stain as possible by absorption, scraping or gentle abrasion before any chemical is applied.
Test an inconspicuous area with the approved product, and judge the result before treating the stain.
Apply an approved stain remover, allow contact time, and work from the outside of the stain toward its centre.
Rinse, blot and check the area, and repeat or refer when the stain remains.
Record the stain, product, test result and outcome for each stain treated or referred.

instruction.heading: Stain removal is a method, not a guess
instruction.body: The aim is a stain-free surface that the customer can use straight away, and a surface that is not damaged in the process. Stain removal follows four principles. First, identify the stain and the material it sits on. Second, test an inconspicuous area before any product touches the stain. Third, use only an approved product and the manufacturer's method. Fourth, record what was done and what happened. The source for this lesson sets these as the working standard, and the source's wording is not reproduced here. Where a source statement reads as a negation of its own steps, this lesson uses the positive principle and the reviewer is asked to confirm the intent.

instruction.heading: Identify the stain and the surface first
instruction.body: Before you choose a method, find out what the stain is, how old it is, and what it is on. The material matters as much as the stain. Some synthetic materials can be damaged by organic solvents, so check the material and the manufacturer's directions before you use a solvent-based product. Some stains need a product chosen for that stain type. If you cannot identify the stain or the material with confidence, do not treat it until the supervisor or the manufacturer's guide has confirmed the method. Stop and identify first, because a wrong product can set a stain or damage a surface.

instruction.heading: Protect yourself and the area
instruction.body: Wear gloves whenever you use a stain remover, a spot treatment or a chewing gum remover, because the product can irritate the skin and the dust on a surface can reach your hands. Open windows or doors where possible so that no one nearby breathes fumes. Set out a barrier around the area, so that dirt is not walked into the damp area and people do not slip. Check that each chemical has its manufacturer's label displayed before you open it, and keep sprays switched off when a container is not in use.

instruction.heading: Remove first, then treat
instruction.body: Take off as much of the stain as you can before any chemical goes on. Use absorption, where you blot up liquid with a clean cloth. Use scraping for solids, carefully and without damaging the surface. Use gentle abrasion only where the surface allows it. Then try water on the stain before any product is applied, because water sometimes lifts a stain without a chemical. Stop if water spreads the stain or changes the surface, and report it.

instruction.heading: Test, treat, work and check
instruction.body: Spot test an unnoticeable area with the approved product before you use it on the stain, and wait for its contact time. Look for any change in colour, texture or the surface itself. If the test area changes, do not use the product on the stain. Once the test is clear, spray the approved product onto the stain and allow the contact time, checking the progress regularly. Work with a small scrubbing brush from the outside of the stain toward the centre, so the stain does not spread outward. Rinse the surface with water, and blot it dry with a white cloth or white paper towel. Check whether the stain has gone. If it is still present, repeat the treatment once, as set out in the procedure, and then refer it if it remains.

instruction.heading: When to stop and refer
instruction.body: A stain must be referred to the supervisor, and not treated further, when the test area changes; when the stain does not respond after the repeat; when you cannot identify the stain or the material; when the stain is on building fabric, such as graffiti or staining on a structure, which may be a separate quoted service; or when a treatment would need a product or method that is not on your approved list. Referral is a sound decision. The record must say why the stain was referred, and what was seen during the test.

instruction.heading: Record the result
instruction.body: Each stain treated or referred needs a record. Write down the location and surface, the stain type, the product name and dilution, the result of the test area, and the outcome. If the stain was not removed, write down what remained and who was told. The recording step is a team documentation rule, and it lets the business show what was done to a customer's surface. Keep the record with the job file.

procedure: Identify the stain type, its age, and the surface or material it is on. If you cannot identify either, stop and refer it.
Check the material for compatibility with any solvent-based product, and check the manufacturer's directions for that material.
Put on gloves, open ventilation where possible, set out the barrier, and check the product label is displayed.
Remove solid matter and excess liquid by absorption, scraping or gentle abrasion, without damaging the surface.
Try water on the stain before any chemical is applied. Stop and refer if the water spreads the stain or changes the surface.
Spot test the approved product on an unnoticeable area, and wait for its contact time. Check the test area for colour change, texture change or damage.
If the test area is clear, spray the approved product onto the stain and allow its contact time.
Work with a small scrubbing brush from the outside of the stain toward the centre, so the stain does not spread.
Check the stain regularly during the contact time. If the product has no effect, stop, do not add more product, and refer.
Rinse the surface with water, and blot it dry with a white cloth or white paper towel.
Check whether the stain has been removed. If it remains, repeat from the test step once. If it still remains, refer it.
Once the area is dry, vacuum the carpet or clean the surface as your business procedure sets out.
Record the location, stain type, product and dilution, test result and outcome, or the reason for referral.
Wash the cloths and buckets, stand buckets upside down to air dry, and store the chemicals with the spray switched off, in their colour groups.

workedExamples.situation: A red drink stain is on a light-coloured carpet. The spot test on an unnoticeable area shows the colour lifting from the test patch.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Do you treat the stain with this product?
workedExamples.reasoning: No. The test area changed, so the product is not suitable for this carpet. Do not use it on the stain. Record the test result, and ask your supervisor for the next approved product or method. Do not try a stronger product to get a better result.

workedExamples.situation: A pen mark is on a timber-look hard floor. The label on the floor cleaner says it contains a solvent.
workedExamples.reasoning: Check the floor material and the manufacturer's directions before using any solvent-based product, because some synthetic finishes can be damaged by solvents. Spot test an unnoticeable area first. If the material is unknown, refer the stain rather than guess.

workedExamples.situation: After two treatments, the stain is faded but still visible, and the customer asks you to keep going until it disappears.
workedExamples.reasoning: Stop. Do not keep applying product, because repeated treatment can damage the surface. Record the stain, the products used, the number of repeats and the result. Tell your supervisor, and follow your business procedure for telling the customer and for any further quoted work.

equipmentAndPpe: Gloves for handling stain removers and spot treatments.
Goggles where splash or spray is possible.
Approved stain removers, each with its manufacturer's label displayed and its safety data sheet available.
Small scrubbing brush for working from the outside to the centre of the stain.
White cloths or white paper towels for rinsing and blotting.
Clean water supply, and absorbent cloths for removing liquid.
Vacuum cleaner for the final clean of carpet.
Barrier and warning signs for the work area.

commonErrors.error: Applying a product to a stain before identifying the stain or the material.
commonErrors.prevention: Identify the stain and the surface first. If either is unknown, stop and refer.

commonErrors.error: Skipping the spot test because the stain looks urgent.
commonErrors.prevention: Always test an unnoticeable area, and wait for the contact time before going on to the stain.

commonErrors.error: Scrubbing from the centre outward, which spreads the stain.
commonErrors.prevention: Work from the outside edge toward the centre with a small brush.

commonErrors.error: Using a stronger product or more product when the first treatment has no effect.
commonErrors.prevention: Use one approved product at its label dilution. If it has no effect, stop and refer.

commonErrors.error: Leaving product residue because the surface was not rinsed and blotted.
commonErrors.prevention: Rinse with water and blot with a white cloth or paper towel before checking.

commonErrors.error: Treating a stain and not recording the test result or the outcome.
commonErrors.prevention: Complete the stain record before you leave the job.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Chemical use follows the manufacturer's label and the safety data sheet for each product. Do not mix products, and do not use a product that is not on the approved list for the surface.
Organic solvents can damage some synthetic materials. Check the material and the manufacturer's directions, and spot test, before using any solvent-based product.
Ventilation: open windows or doors where possible so that no one nearby breathes fumes from a stain remover.
Slips: a damp carpet or floor is a slip hazard. Use barrier and warning signs until the surface is confirmed dry.
Stain removal on building fabric, such as graffiti or staining on a structure, is not covered by this lesson.

qualityStandard: Stain and surface identified and recorded before any product is applied.
Test area checked, with no colour change, texture change or damage, before the approved product is used on the stain.
Stain removed, or referred with the reason recorded.
Surface rinsed, blotted and dry, with no product residue or ring left behind.
Equipment washed, colour-coded and stored with chemical sprays switched off.
documentationEvidence: Stain record: location, surface or material, stain type, age if known.
Product record: product name, dilution, contact time and the test-area result.
Outcome record: removed, partly removed or referred, and the reason for any referral.
Before and after photographs, where the business's quality rules require them.
Equipment wash and colour-group check record.
summary: Identify the stain and the material before you choose a method.
Remove as much as you can first, and try water before any chemical.
Spot test an unnoticeable area with the approved product, and judge the result before you treat the stain.
Work from the outside of the stain toward the centre, then rinse and blot.
Stop and refer when the test changes, the stain does not respond, or you cannot identify it.
Record the stain, the product, the test result and the outcome every time.

knowledgeChecks.question: What do you do before applying a stain remover to a stain?
options: Spray it straight onto the stain so that it works faster on the fabric
Spot test an inconspicuous area with the approved product, and check the result
Mix it with a second product so that the stain lifts in one pass

knowledgeChecks.question: Which direction should you work in when you brush a stain?
options: From the outside edge toward the centre, so the stain does not spread
From the centre outward, so the edges are reached quickly
Across the whole stain at once, starting from the middle

knowledgeChecks.question: After two treatments the stain is still visible, and the test area has changed colour. What should you do?
options: Use a stronger product on the stain until it disappears and keep rubbing
Rinse with hot water and dry the area quickly and try a second product
Stop, record the outcome, and refer it to the supervisor for a decision
